clue.text: Memorial of Bennett

definitions.meaning: a monument raised in honour of someone
A play by Arnold Bennett, written with Eden Phillpotts

explanation.surface: A monument raised in memory of someone called Bennett.
explanation.definitionFit: A carved figure set up in a public place commemorates its subject, and Bennett's play bears that title.

clue.text: Hungry boy asks for another card

definitions.meaning: Dickens's Oliver, the workhouse orphan who famously asks for more gruel
in the card game pontoon, a player wanting one more card says this word

explanation.surface: A hungry lad requests an extra card at the gaming table.
explanation.walkthrough: In pontoon (blackjack), calling for one more card is the verb used here; the clue's 'asks for another card' describes saying it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's starving orphan bears this surname, and in pontoon the word is the call for a further card.

clue.text: Doyle's patient doctor and renowned historian

definitions.meaning: Dr Percy ... is the physician in the Sherlock Holmes story The Resident Patient
G. M. ... wrote English Social History

explanation.surface: A doctor with a patient in a Conan Doyle tale is also a famous historian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient doctor' reads as a doctor with patience, but it means the doctor of Doyle's story The Resident Patient.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to the physician in Doyle's story and to the eminent Cambridge historian George Macaulay.

clue.text: Traces of travel brought back from the East

definitions.text: Traces of travel brought back from the East

parts.words: Traces of travel brought back from the East
parts.note: close to the subtitle of A. W. Kinglake's 1844 travel book, whose Greek title itself means from the East

explanation.surface: Souvenirs a traveller carries home from Eastern lands.
explanation.walkthrough: Kinglake's book is subtitled 'Traces of Travel Brought Home from the East', and its Greek title means 'from the East'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinglake's classic account of journeys through the Levant carries this Greek title and that subtitle.

clue.text: Rejected, we're told, like the work of Cozzens

definitions.meaning: something thrown aside is said to be ...
A 1934 novel by James Gould Cozzens

explanation.surface: A rejected manuscript, like one of Cozzens's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Something discarded has been cast away, and Cozzens titled a novel of a man marooned in a department store so.

clue.text: Stories from Kentish Town

parts.note: the town is the cathedral city in Kent where Chaucer's pilgrims are heading, not the London district called Kentish Town

explanation.surface: Tales collected in the London district of Kentish Town.
explanation.walkthrough: Kentish Town is a district of north London, but here it means a town in the county of Kent: the cathedral city of Chaucer's pilgrimage.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's pilgrims tell their stories on the road to the Kent cathedral city, giving the collection its name.

clue.text: Frank Yerby suggests something should be said at once

definitions.meaning: A 1969 novel by the American writer Frank Yerby

definitions.text: something should be said at once

explanation.surface: A frank remark hints that something must be said straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like the adjective for candid speech, but it is the novelist's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Yerby's novel bears this title, and the phrase is an instruction to talk immediately, as in a wedding service's challenge.

clue.text: Playboy caused riots at this playhouse

definitions.text: Playboy caused riots at this playhouse

parts.words: Playboy caused riots at this playhouse
parts.note: Synge's The Playboy of the Western World provoked riots at its 1907 premiere in Dublin's national theatre

explanation.surface: A womaniser stirred up a riot in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playboy' suggests a rake, but it is Synge's play, whose 1907 Dublin opening set off riots.
explanation.definitionFit: Dublin's national theatre, founded by Yeats and Lady Gregory, staged Synge's play and saw the riots.

clue.text: Directions given by Emerson with lectures

definitions.meaning: the details written on envelopes saying where letters go
Emerson published a volume titled Nature

explanation.surface: Emerson hands out instructions along with his lectures.
explanation.definitionFit: Destination details on mail are so called, and Emerson's speeches were collected with his lectures under that word.

clue.text: "Sir Patrick O'Prism, a — painter of high renown" (Thomas Love Peacock)

definitions.text: "Sir Patrick O'Prism, a — painter of high renown" (Thomas Love Peacock)

parts.words: "Sir Patrick O'Prism, a — painter of high renown" (Thomas Love Peacock)
parts.note: the dash stands for the missing word in Peacock's description of a character in Headlong Hall, an amateur dabbler in art

explanation.surface: A quotation from Peacock's satire describing the painter Sir Patrick O'Prism.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver supplies the missing word in Peacock's line from Headlong Hall: the painter is an amateur of the arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Peacock's O'Prism is an amateur who dabbles in painting, a lover of the arts rather than a professional.

clue.text: Kirkup's servant

parts.note: James Kirkup's poetry collection The ... Servant supplies the first word of a phrase for a personal valet

explanation.surface: A servant employed by someone called Kirkup.
explanation.walkthrough: James Kirkup published The Body Servant (1971); a 'body servant' is a personal attendant.
explanation.definitionFit: A personal valet is called a body servant, and Kirkup's collection takes that phrase as its title.

clue.text: Example in there by English playwright

indicators.note: the word there is set within the two letters of the example abbreviation

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
taken as written

explanation.surface: An example, there, by an English dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is loose: the letters of THERE go inside EG to make ETHEREG, and E for English follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir George Etherege was the Restoration dramatist who wrote The Man of Mode.

clue.text: Economist is punishing, they say

indicators.note: signals that the word for punishing is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: canes means beats with a stick, so punishes

explanation.surface: An economist is said to be a harsh disciplinarian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They say' marks a homophone: CANES, punishes with a stick, sounds like the economist's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: John Maynard Keynes was the British economist behind the General Theory.

clue.text: Found on verge by Cornish poet

definitions.text: Found on verge by Cornish poet

parts.words: Found on verge by Cornish poet
parts.note: Jack Clemo, the Cornish poet, titled a collection The ... Verge, after the china-... country

explanation.surface: Something a Cornish poet came across at the roadside.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cornish poet Jack Clemo wrote The Clay Verge (1951), named after the china-clay pits of mid-Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: Clemo's collection title puts this earthy material beside the verge, and china clay is Cornwall's great industry.

clue.text: Shaw's French maid

parts.note: Joan of Arc, heroine of Shaw's Saint Joan, was known by the French title meaning the Maid

explanation.surface: A French maidservant employed by Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French maid' suggests a domestic, but it is Joan of Arc, called the Maid in French, heroine of Saint Joan.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan of Arc was hailed in French as the Maid of Orléans, and Shaw made her the subject of Saint Joan.

clue.text: Reserve stake in former carrier

parts.note: to book is to reserve a place
a post is a stake driven into the ground

explanation.surface: Booking a stake on a former airline or shipper.
explanation.walkthrough: Book post was a cheap postal rate for sending printed matter, now discontinued.
explanation.definitionFit: The old reduced postal service for printed matter delivered books and papers.

clue.text: … water-colours I never should have done at all, except for the long continuance of a necessity for - (D. G. Rossetti, Letters)

definitions.text: … water-colours I never should have done at all, except for the long continuance of a necessity for - (D. G. Rossetti, Letters)

parts.words: … water-colours I never should have done at all, except for the long continuance of a necessity for - (D. G. Rossetti, Letters)
parts.note: Rossetti says he painted these water-colours only for money, so the gap needs a word for hack work done to pay the bills

explanation.surface: Rossetti complains in a letter that he painted water-colours only from need.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the dash: Rossetti painted the water-colours to earn a living, which is what the hyphenated word means.
explanation.definitionFit: Work produced only to keep the pot boiling, that is to earn a living, is so called.

clue.text: His belief in perfection is Tao put differently

definitions.text: His belief in perfection is Tao put differently

indicators.note: put differently tells us the letters of is, Tao and put are arranged anew

explanation.surface: A man's faith in perfection is merely Taoism restated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Differently' rearranges IS, TAO and PUT into the answer; the whole clue also describes the person, one whose belief in perfection is like the Tao.
explanation.definitionFit: A believer in an ideal perfect society, after More's Utopia, is so called.

clue.text: Sylvia Ashton-Warner's unmatched protagonist

parts.note: Ashton-Warner's 1958 novel about a teacher is titled after its unmarried heroine; unmatched means not wedded

explanation.surface: Praise for a novelist's peerless heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unmatched' reads as peerless, but means unmarried: Ashton-Warner's novel Spinster is about an unmarried teacher in New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashton-Warner's heroine, an unwed teacher, gives the novel its title.

clue.text: Job offered by Cowper

definitions.meaning: a piece of work to be done
William Cowper's long blank-verse poem is The ...

explanation.surface: A post advertised by Cowper.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of work to be done is a chore, and Cowper's long 1785 poem is titled after one.

clue.text: Alexander, Catherine, perhaps, in honours examination

definitions.meaning: Alexander the Great and Catherine the Great are examples of rulers with this epithet
at Oxford, the final classics honours course and exam is so named

explanation.surface: Alexander and Catherine sitting a university honours exam.
explanation.walkthrough: Greats is the Oxford name for the Literae Humaniores degree course and its final exams.
explanation.definitionFit: Rulers such as Alexander and Catherine carry the epithet, and Oxford's classics finals bear the same nickname.

clue.text: Shakespearean knight gets credit on nothing in concession

indicators.note: the credit and nothing letters go inside the word for a concession

parts.note: a sop is a small concession to appease someone
CR is the accountancy abbreviation for credit
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean knight gets credit on nothing as a favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' means CR comes before O; together they go 'in' SOP. Sir Stephen Scroop appears in Richard II.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Stephen Scroop is the loyal knight who brings bad news to Richard II.

clue.text: Dramatist in a minor tone

indicators.note: the dramatist's name lies inside the run of letters of minor tone

explanation.surface: A playwright writing in a minor key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points inside the words: minOR TONe holds the name of Joe Orton, author of Loot.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Orton was the English playwright of Loot and Entertaining Mr Sloane.

clue.text: One of Lawrence's shellbacks

parts.note: D. H. Lawrence wrote a sequence of poems about these armoured reptiles

explanation.surface: An old sailor among Lawrence's crew.
explanation.walkthrough: A shellback is an old sailor, but here it is a creature with a shell on its back, as in Lawrence's poems in Birds, Beasts and Flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence's sequence of poems in Birds, Beasts and Flowers is about this slow shelled reptile.

clue.text: Millet's peasant more than once employed by Van Gogh

definitions.text: Millet's peasant more than once employed by Van Gogh

parts.words: Millet's peasant more than once employed by Van Gogh
parts.note: Millet's painting of a man scattering seed was copied and reworked several times by Van Gogh

explanation.surface: A farm labourer of Millet's later hired by Van Gogh.
explanation.walkthrough: Millet painted a peasant broadcasting seed (1850), and Van Gogh made several versions of the figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure scattering seed in Millet's painting gives it its title, and Van Gogh painted it repeatedly.

clue.text: Essential device in conspiracy novels

parts.note: the story line of any novel, and also a word for a conspiracy

explanation.surface: A key element in conspiracy thrillers.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a scheme of conspirators and the storyline of a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Every novel needs a storyline, and conspirators hatch a scheme: one word covers both.

clue.text: Shall allow new description of Williams's preceding day

indicators.note: new shows the letters of shall allow make a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A new permission granted for describing a day in Williams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges SHALL ALLOW. Charles Williams's novel All Hallows' Eve names the eve, the day preceding this feast.
explanation.definitionFit: All Saints' Day is the feast whose eve gave Charles Williams his title, so the term describes the day after his.

clue.text: Shakespearean "poor but worthy gentleman", born by lion sign

parts.note: Leo is the lion sign of the zodiac
natus is Latin for born

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean gentleman, poor but worthy, born under Leo.
explanation.walkthrough: Posthumus Leonatus, hero of Cymbeline, is described as 'a poor but worthy gentleman'; his name means 'lion-born', which the soothsayer explains.
explanation.definitionFit: Posthumus, Imogen's husband in Cymbeline, carries this surname and is called a poor but worthy gentleman.

clue.text: Rarest form of French philosopher

indicators.note: a form of the word rarest means its letters in another shape

explanation.surface: The rarest kind of French thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form of' rearranges RAREST into the name of Jean-Paul, the existentialist.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Paul Sartre was the French existentialist philosopher of Being and Nothingness.
